source_reviews.independent_solution: Forced electrical oscillations occur when an external source maintains a periodically varying electromotive force or voltage across a connected circuit, producing periodically changing current and charge. The external drive supplies energy repeatedly; this is not merely an initially charged isolated capacitor undergoing free oscillations. Once transients die away, the forced oscillation frequency is the driving frequency. Equality to the circuit's natural frequency is a resonance condition, not a necessary condition for forced oscillations.
source_reviews.required_task: State the external periodic driving condition, not just the existence of stored charge, constant voltage or a natural-frequency coincidence.

source_reviews.independent_solution: For a fixed pure resistance R>0, instantaneous Ohm's law gives u(t)=R i(t), hence i(t)=u(t)/R. If u(t)=U_m sin(omega t+phi), then i(t)=(U_m/R) sin(omega t+phi). Current and voltage have the same frequency and phase: their zeros, signs and corresponding extrema occur together. Therefore I_m=U_m/R and, on the same averaging interval, I=U/R. These same-phase relations do not hold unchanged for arbitrary circuits containing inductance or capacitance.
source_reviews.required_task: Relate instantaneous current and voltage, proportionality and phase in the purely resistive circuit.

source_reviews.independent_solution: For a sinusoid averaged over whole periods, <u^2>=U_m^2 <sin^2>=U_m^2/2. Thus U=U_m/sqrt(2) and the nonnegative peak amplitude is U_m=sqrt(2) U. The 220 V RMS line has amplitude 220 sqrt(2) V = 311.1269837220809 V, approximately 311 V. The 127 V RMS line has amplitude 127 sqrt(2) V = 179.60512242138307 V, approximately 180 V. Neither RMS value is itself the peak, and dividing the given RMS values by sqrt(2) reverses the requested conversion. This is a paper calculation, not an instruction to measure a live circuit.
source_reviews.required_task: Calculate both voltage amplitudes from their respective RMS values under the stated sinusoidal condition, preserving the order and volts.

source_reviews.independent_solution: For a specified time interval of duration Delta t>0, define I=sqrt((1/Delta t) integral i(t)^2 dt) and U=sqrt((1/Delta t) integral u(t)^2 dt), taking the nonnegative roots. The squared instantaneous quantities remain inside the time average. For periodic AC the customary RMS values use a complete period or whole periods. Since resistor power is R i(t)^2=u(t)^2/R, a constant DC current of magnitude I or DC voltage of magnitude U gives the same average heating on the same fixed resistance over that interval. This is not equality of instantaneous current or voltage. A symmetric sinusoid has zero signed mean but nonzero RMS, and peak/sqrt(2) is a sinusoidal whole-period result, not a definition for all waveforms.
source_reviews.required_task: Define both current and voltage RMS, including operation order, nonnegative root, averaging interval and heating interpretation without replacing RMS by signed mean or a universal peak conversion.
